opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think for me it came from a pretty simple place. When I was younger, I got really drawn into the idea that there's a small set of rules that explain an enormous amount of what you see in the world. Physics felt like the most fundamental version of that. Chemistry sits on top of physics, biology sits on top of chemistry, and so on. So if you wanted to understand how things actually work at the deepest level, it seemed like that was where you had to start.

There was also something romantic about it. You read about people like Einstein, Feynman, or the folks who built quantum mechanics, and it seemed like the place where the most profound intellectual breakthroughs happened. A handful of people, armed mostly with math and a few key experiments, completely changed how humanity understood reality. As a kid, that was incredibly compelling. I wanted to work on the hardest, most foundational problems.

What I didn't fully appreciate at the time was that the frontier of a field matters as much as how fundamental it is. When I got deep into physics research, I realized many of the big questions were either extremely hard to make progress on or had become very incremental. You could spend years on a narrow problem that might move things a little bit. Meanwhile, I started noticing that deep learning had the feeling physics must have had in the early twentieth century. There were huge open questions, things were moving fast, and a small group of people could have an outsized impact.

So, in a way, physics taught me how to think. It taught me to look for simple principles, to be comfortable with math, and to build models of complicated systems. But it also made me realize that what I really cared about was being at the place where the most fundamental progress was happening at that moment. For me, that ended up being AI.

fable-5.1.text:
I think when I was a kid I had this feeling that physics was the one discipline where you could actually get to the bottom of things. Most fields take some set of assumptions as given and build on top of them. Physics was the place where you didn't have to accept the assumptions, you could keep asking why until you hit the actual rules of the universe. That felt like the most fundamental thing a person could spend their life on.

Part of it was also the people. I grew up reading about Feynman and Einstein and that whole generation, and they seemed to approach the world with this mix of rigor and playfulness. They weren't just solving problems, they were trying to understand reality from first principles, and they had a lot of fun doing it. I wanted to be like that.

And honestly, as a teenager I thought the questions that mattered most were the deep ones. What is space, what is time, what is matter made of. Physics was the discipline that had earned the right to answer those questions, because it actually produced results you could check against the world. So if you cared about truth, that seemed like the root of the tree. Everything else felt downstream of it.

What I didn't appreciate at the time, and only came to later, is that there's another kind of fundamental question, which is what intelligence is and how it works. That ended up pulling me in a different direction, but the instinct was the same. I wanted to work on whatever felt like the deepest open problem.

astra-6.text:
I think what drew me to physics was the idea that you could explain a lot with a little. You have this incredibly complicated world, but underneath it there might be a small set of principles that let you understand what’s going on. That felt very powerful to me.

And I liked the combination of intuition and rigor. You could ask a really basic question—why does something behave the way it does?—and then push beyond a verbal explanation to something precise, something you could test. Physics seemed like the place where you could take that instinct as far as possible.

sol-6.1.text:
I was drawn to physics because I wanted to understand things at the most fundamental level. You look at the complexity of the world, and somehow a relatively small set of principles can explain so much of it. That was incredibly appealing to me.

And I liked the way of thinking: you start with a complicated problem, figure out what matters, and build the simplest model that captures it. Even if you end up working on something other than physics, that instinct—to get underneath the surface and ask what’s actually driving the behavior—is really valuable.
